teaser: The vault behind this newsroom, 35,000 objects and ten agents, measured eight ways: one folder in 13 seconds, history as the edge, storage as the bottleneck.
core_idea: The vault the newsroom's ten agents share, 1,295 commits, 5,281 files and 35,000 encrypted objects, is the size of a real application's source repository; a full clone takes three and a half minutes but an agent takes one folder with one commit in 13 seconds and 3 MB, a file on demand in under 3, a pull in 2.5; without a depth a partial clone walks history one request per commit, a fix is designed; and from local disk the same clone is 0.8 seconds, so the time is the storage, which makes sgit plausible for source code.

quotes.text: A clone that carries a depth costs seconds and megabytes however large the vault is
So sgit is not the bottleneck; the distance to the storage is.

figures.caption: The newsroom's vault against two of our own git repositories: 5,281 files, 1,295 commits and 35,423 objects, against the SG/Send application's 5,584 files, 4,399 commits and 42,434 objects, and the sgit CLI's 1,811 files, 1,603 commits and 13,985 objects.

What an agent fetches from the 35,000-object vault and what it costs, on a log scale: the full clone 210 seconds; the whole tree with one commit 57; one 130-file folder with one commit 13 seconds and 137 objects; structure only 27; one folder with all its history 227; the biggest folder with all its history 264; widening a clone by a folder 7.8; one file on demand 2.9; a pull with nothing new 2.5.

The same vault and client with the objects in three places: hosted, a plain file server on local disk, and a local API server. Full clone 210, 111 and 69 seconds; one commit 57, 25 and 12; one folder with one commit 13, 2.3 and 0.8; one folder with all history 181 hosted against 7.1 locally; one file on demand 2.5, 1.8 and 1.8.
